issues.issue: A 190-day maximum dollar-weighted average maturity sits against c055's five-year maximum maturity for an individual security and c052's "shortest of" deeming rules, which can make long instruments count as very short. Whether the average is a real constraint on duration is contestable.

The special rule for variable rate demand obligations overlaps the general "shortest of" rule in c052, which already covers interest-rate resets and put dates. Which rule governs an instrument answering both descriptions is not stated.

"Whichever is earlier" makes the deferral expire at six months even before any assets are invested, which reads as a slip for "later" and reverses the clause's evident sense. The mechanical choice of word decides when the 190-day limit bites.

This clause defers the maturity requirement until the six-month or $100 million trigger, "whichever is earlier," while the identically worded diversification deferral (c050) says "whichever is later." The two cannot both reflect the same intended scheme.

A five-year maximum maturity is hard to reconcile with the Portfolio Quality rule (c043) permitting only obligations with the highest short-term rating and with the daily-liquidity objective in c039. Which provision limits the other is a genuine question on the whole instrument.

"The industry convention for these types of securities will be used" imports an unidentified external standard for weighted average life, with no source named and no tie-breaker if conventions differ. The maximum maturity of a whole class of holdings turns on that undefined phrase.

The clause turns on "Unrated Security," a capitalised term defined nowhere in the memorandum, and on whether the security "presents minimal credit risks" — with the remedial step left wholly to what "the Investment Manager determines is in the best interests" of the Trust. There is no ascertainable duty to sell or hold.

Allowing a downgraded security to be retained at the manager's discretion is in tension with c043's statement that the Trust "may only invest in" obligations with the highest short-term rating. Whether the quality restriction is a continuing or purchase-time-only test is left open.

Permitting the Trustee to invest "all of the assets" of the CI Term Trust in another series is hard to square with the 5% single-issuer limit (c045), the 15% illiquid cap (c046) and the daily-liquidity objective (c039), since another series' units are private placement interests. Reading it literally would nullify the diversification guidelines.

"A leading money market index such as Fed Funds or LIBOR" pairs an open-ended general standard with two examples, leaving unclear whether other indices qualify and what makes one "leading." The permissible index set cannot be read off the words.

The credit-risk description refers to "the counterparty to a derivative," although derivatives appear nowhere in the permitted-investment list (c044) and dual index and inverse floaters are prohibited by c064. The mismatch could be used to argue the permitted universe is wider than the list suggests.

The acknowledgement that illiquid holdings may prevent sale at an advantageous time or price cuts against the investment objective in c039, which makes daily liquidity a prime consideration. A court could be asked whether the risk disclosure qualifies the objective or vice versa.

Reliance on Rule 506 of Regulation D (which turns on accredited investors) is stated alongside c075's reliance on Section 3(c)(7) (which requires "qualified purchasers") and c001's offer to "qualified institutional purchasers." The instrument gives three different investor-eligibility criteria without reconciling them.

The exemption is premised on Shares being owned only by "qualified purchasers," whereas c001 offers Shares to "qualified institutional purchasers" and the cover page addresses "qualified institutional or accredited investors." Which class of investor may in fact hold Shares is left inconsistent across the document.

The statement that no ERISA Plan investors are anticipated is difficult to square with c003, which describes the Trust's purpose as serving securities-lending clients of Wells Fargo as lending agent, a class that commonly includes ERISA plans. Whether Plan money may be invested is left unresolved.

Saying Wells Fargo merely "intends to restrict transfers of ownership" presupposes some transfers are possible, while c027 states flatly that Shares "may not be transferred or assigned." The two provisions describe different transfer regimes.

Describing the Memorandum as merely "an overview of the CI Term Trust and its policies" pulls against c042's mandatory direction that investments "shall comply with the following portfolio guidelines." Whether the guidelines are contractually binding or only descriptive is precisely what this tension raises.

The return obligation is triggered by three disjunctive events ("upon delivery of updated offering materials, upon reaching a decision not to subscribe, or if such subscription is not accepted"), none of which addresses a recipient who does subscribe and is accepted. The clause's operation in that case cannot be read off its words.
